rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meccan leaders, or alternatively Uyayna b. Hisn and his party, asked Muhammad to dismiss poor believers such as Ammar, Suhayb, Salman, Ibn Masud, and Bilal; Ibn Atiyya prefers the Meccan leaders because the sura is Meccan.
rows.anchor: عظماء الكفار قيل من أهل مكة، وقيل عيينة بن حصن وأصحابه والأول أصوب، لأن السورة مكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The leaders complained that the poor companions' clothes smelled and demanded their removal before they would sit with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: يريدون عمار بن ياسر وصهيب بن سنان وسلمان الفارسي وابن مسعود وغيرهم من الفقراء كبلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say the Prophet sat with the poor believers and praised God for commanding him to be patient with them, welcoming those for whom his Lord reproached him.
rows.anchor: خرج إليهم وجلس بينهم، وقال الحمد لله الذي جعل من أمتي من أمرت أن أصبر نفسي معه

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: Salman reports that Uyayna, al-Aqra, and their companions, described as those whose hearts were reconciled, made the same demand, prompting the verse.
rows.anchor: وروى سلمان أن المؤلفة قلوبهم، عيينة بن حصن والأقرع بن حابس وذويهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report about the reconciled leaders could make the verse Medinan, but Ibn Atiyya thinks it was likely Meccan and a reply to Quraysh.
rows.anchor: فالآية على هذا مدنية، ويشبه أن تكون الآية مكية، وفعل المؤلفة قريش فرد بالآية عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ṣbir means to hold or restrain oneself; the related term describes an animal held as a target, which the Prophet forbade.
rows.anchor: واصبر معناه احبس، ومنه المصبورة التي جاء فيها الحديث: نهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن صبر الحيوان

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read al-ghadati; Ibn Amir and several early readers read al-ghudwati, despite the latter's grammatical weakness because ghudwa is a known proper noun.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور «بالغداة» ، وقرأ ابن عامر «بالغدوة» وهي قراءة نصر بن عاصم ومالك بن دينار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif-lam in al-ghudwa can be explained as making the time word indefinite or generic, as in al-fina, so the reading has a possible defense.
rows.anchor: وجه القراءة بذلك أنهم ألحقوها ضربا من التنكير إذ قالوا حيث غدوة يريدون الغدوات

rows.speaker: ابن عمر ومجاهد وإبراهيم
rows.claim: The morning and evening invocation refers to the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: الإشارة بقوله يدعون ربهم بالغداة والعشي إلى الصلوات الخمس. قاله ابن عمر ومجاهد وإبراهيم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The morning-and-evening invocation specifically means the dawn and afternoon prayers.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة المراد صلاة الفجر، وصلاة العصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also includes people who invoke God outside prayer and those who gather to study religious knowledge.
rows.anchor: ويدخل في الآية من يدعو في غير صلاة، ومن يجتمع لمذاكرة علم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says remembering God morning and evening is better than breaking swords in God's path or freely giving wealth.
rows.anchor: روى عبد الله بن عمر عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال «لذكر الله بالغداة والعشي أفضل من حطم السيوف

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن
rows.claim: Abu Abd al-Rahman read al-ghudu without the final h; Ibn Abi Abla read the morning and evening terms as plurals.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عبد الرحمن «بالغدو» دون هاء، وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة «بالغدوات» «والعشيات» على الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not turning one's eyes from the believers means not looking past them toward worldly people and the clothing of disbelievers.
rows.anchor: أي لا تتجاوز عنهم إلى أبناء الدنيا والملابس من الكفار

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan's first reading uses a form that makes the Prophet the one who must not turn his eyes away; another variant has a still ʿayn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن «ولا تعد عينيك» بضم التاء وفتح العين وشد الدال المكسورة

rows.speaker: خباب
rows.claim: Khabbab identifies the heedless person as Uyayna b. Hisn and al-Aqra; another interpretation takes the description generally.
rows.anchor: قيل إنه أراد بذلك معينا وهو عيينة بن حصن، والأقرع قاله خباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the initial target is Quraysh disbelievers, since the verse is Meccan, while the wording can apply to anyone of this character.
rows.anchor: وقيل إنما أراد من هذه صفته، وإنما المراد أولا كفار قريش، لأن الآية مكية

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority reading takes the heart as the accusative object: God made it heedless; another reading means that the person neglected remembrance and abandoned it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «أغفلنا قلبه» بنصب الباء على معنى جعلناه غافلا

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: A variant attributed by al-Dani to Amr b. Ubayd understands the phrase as someone who neglected God's remembrance and left it.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو عمرو الداني أنها قراءة عمرو بن عبيد

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni explains the reading as meaning someone whom we supposed to be heedless of Us.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جني المعنى من ظننا غافلين عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farata may mean neglect and waste of duty, or excess and extravagance; exegetes used both senses, while Khabbab, Dawud, and Ibn Zayd gave related glosses.
rows.anchor: و «الفرط» يحتمل أن يكون بمعنى التفريط والتضييع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truth from the Lord may mean the Quran itself, or the Prophet's refusal to obey the elites and his patience with the believers.
rows.anchor: هذا الحق من ربكم أي هذا القرآن، أو هذا الإعراض عنكم، وترك الطاعة لكم

rows.speaker: قعنب وأبو السمال
rows.claim: Qunab and Abu al-Sammal read qul with a fatḥa on the lām; Abu Hatim judges this poor Arabic.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قعنب وأبو السمال «وقل» بفتح اللام قال أبو حاتم وذلك رديء في العربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commands to believe or disbelieve are a threat: each person is challenged to choose what he will find with God.
rows.anchor: فمن شاء فليؤمن الآية توعد وتهديد، أي فليختر كل امرئ لنفسه ما يجده غدا عند الله

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group construes the choice as governed by God's will: whom He wills to believe believes, and whom He wills to disbelieve disbelieves.
rows.anchor: وتأولت فرقة فمن شاء الله إيمانه فليؤمن ومن شاء الله كفره فليكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya accepts that construal, while explaining that faith or disbelief is the person's due and that human acquisition grounds reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: ومن حيث للإنسان في ذلك التكسب الذي به يتعلق ثواب الإيمان وعقاب الكفر

rows.speaker: الحسن وعيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Isa al-Thaqafi read the lām in both commands with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعيسى الثقفي «فليؤمن» «وليكفر» بكسر اللامين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿtadna derives from ʿatād, something prepared and ready at hand; surādq is an enclosing wall or tent-like surround.
rows.anchor: وأعتدنا مأخوذ من العتاد وهو الشيء المعد الحاضر و «السرادق» وهو الجدار المحيط

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾba's verse uses surādq for an enclosure, supporting the word's concrete sense.
rows.anchor: يا حكم بن المنذر بن الجارود ... سرادق والمجد عليك ممدود

rows.speaker: سلامة بن جندل
rows.claim: Salama b. Jandal uses musardaq for an enclosed structure, another poetic witness to the word.
rows.anchor: هو المولج النعمان بيتا سماؤه ... صدور الفيول بعد بيت مسردق

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines surādq broadly as anything that surrounds something.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج «السرادق» كل ما أحاط بشيء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya considers surādq more specific than al-Zajjaj's definition of anything enclosing anything.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي أبو محمد: وهو عندي أخص مما قال الزجاج

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Hell's enclosure is a wall of fire; another group says it is smoke surrounding the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: واختلف في «سرادق» النار فقال ابن عباس سرادقها حائط من نار

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group interprets the enclosure as smoke surrounding the disbelievers and connects it with the three-branched shade in al-Mursalat.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة سرادقها دخان يحيط بالكفار

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group places the enclosure in this world and identifies it with the sea; a report from the Prophet through Yaʿla b. Umayya says the sea is Hell.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة الإحاطة هي في الدنيا، والسرادق البحر، وروي هذا المعنى عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من طريق يعلى بن أمية

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: A report from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri says Hell's enclosure has four walls, each forty years' journey wide.
rows.anchor: وروي عنه أيضا عليه السلام من طريق أبي سعيد الخدري أنه قال «سرادق النار أربعة جدور، كتف عرض كل جدار مسيرة أربعين سنة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yughāthū means they are given something that serves as relief, as in a poet's ironic description of a painful blow as a greeting.
rows.anchor: وقوله عز وجل يغاثوا أي يكون لهم مقام الغوث وهذا نحو قول الشاعر:

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid reports from the Prophet that muhl is the dregs of oil heated to its limit.
rows.anchor: و «المهل» قال أبو سعيد عن النبي عليه السلام هو دردي الزيت إذا انتهى حده

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Other explanations of muhl include any liquid heated to its extreme, molten gold, silver, or lead, and a mixture of pus and blood.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة هو كل مائع سخن حتى انتهى حره

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud compared muhl with molten metal by melting a gold or silver vessel and showing its colors to people in Kufa.
rows.anchor: وروي أن عبد الله بن مسعود أهديت إليه سقاية من ذهب أو فضة فأمر بها فأذيبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic report describes the drink burning a disbeliever's face before it is swallowed and cutting his intestines after drinking.
rows.anchor: روي في معناه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال تقرب الشربة من الكافر، فإذا دنت منه تكرهها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Murtfaq generally means something from which comfort is sought; the narrower sense is a reclining place, while Mujahid calls it a gathering place and al-Tabari rejects that gloss.
rows.anchor: والأظهر عندي أن يكون «المرتفق» بمعنى الشيء الذي يطلب رفقه باتكاء وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orchard is singular because the man cannot enter both gardens at the same time.
rows.anchor: أفرد الجنة من حيث الوجود كذلك، إذ لا يدخلهما معا في وقت واحد

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: The man's wronging of himself means disbelief and corrupt beliefs, including doubt about resurrection.
rows.anchor: «ظلمه لنفسه» : كفره وعقائده الفاسدة في الشك في البعث، فقد نص على ذلك قتادة وابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the man's reference is to the cosmos, his doubt concerns its created order; if only to his orchard, it is shallow arrogance and excessive self-delusion.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت إشارته إلى جنته فقط، فإنما في الكلام تساخف واغترار مفرط وقلة تحصيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He wrongly infers from worldly prosperity that he deserves honor, then projects his worldly standing onto the afterlife; Ibn Atiyya distinguishes this from al-As b. Waʾil's deliberate mockery of Khabbab.
rows.anchor: وظن أنه لم يمل له في دنياه إلا لكرامة يستوجبها في نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وابن الزبير
rows.claim: These readers and the Madinan codices have minhuma, referring to the two gardens mentioned earlier.
rows.anchor: وثبت في مصاحف المدينة «منهما» يريد الجنتين المذكورتين أولا

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: These readers and the Basran codex have minha, referring to the single garden he entered.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي والعامة، وكذلك هو مصحف أهل البصرة «منها» يريد الجنة المدخولة

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy b. Kaʿb reads the companion as disputing with the unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي بن كعب: «وهو يخاصمه»

rows.speaker: ثابت البناني
rows.claim: Thabit al-Bunani reads an added rebuke: Woe to you, have you disbelieved?
rows.anchor: وقرأ ثابت البناني، «ويلك أكفرت»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: From dust points to Adam; making him a man may simply mean a person or living being, or may highlight the blessing of being male, as al-Tabari also suggests.
rows.anchor: وقوله من تراب إشارة إلى آدم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari prefers lakin in connected reading and lakinna when pausing, as in Warsh's and Qalun's transmission from Nafi.
rows.anchor: ورجحها الطبري، وهي رواية ورش وقالون عن نافع

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وأبي بن كعب والحسن
rows.claim: This group reads lakin ana huwa Allah rabbi.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود وأبي بن كعب والحسن «لكن أنا هو الله ربي»

rows.speaker: عيسى الثقفي والأعمش
rows.claim: A variant from Isa al-Thaqafi and, in one transmission, al-Aʿmash reads lakin huwa Allah rabbi; Ibn Atiyya discusses several competing grammatical analyses of lakinna.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى الثقفي والأعمش بخلاف «لكن هو الله ربي»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer's lawla is an exhortation meaning why did you not say this when entering your garden?
rows.anchor: وصية من المؤمن للكافر، ولولا تحضيض، بمعنى هلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ma shāʾ Allāh can be a relative clause, a condition, or a report with an omitted subject such as the matter is what God willed.
rows.anchor: وما يحتمل أن تكون بمعنى الذي، بتقدير الذي إن شاء الله كائن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: La quwwata illa billah expresses surrender and opposes the unbeliever's claim that his garden will never perish.
rows.anchor: وقوله لا قوة إلا بالله تسليم وضد لقول الكافر ما أظن أن تبيد هذه أبدا

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet taught Abu Hurayra la quwwata illa billah as a treasure from Paradise and says God calls the speaker His surrendered servant.
rows.anchor: وروي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال لأبي هريرة «ألا أدلك على كلمة من كنز الجنة؟»

rows.speaker: أبو موسى
rows.claim: A report to Abu Musa gives the fuller formula la hawla wa la quwwata illa billahi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿazim as a treasure of Paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أبي موسى: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال له

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir retains the yā in tarani in both connected and paused reading; Ibn Amir, Asim, and Hamza omit it in both.
rows.anchor: فأثبتها ابن كثير وصلا ووقفا، وحذفها ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة فيهما

rows.speaker: نافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Nafi and Abu Amr retain the yā in connection only.
rows.anchor: وأثبتها نافع وأبو عمرو في الوصل فقط

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read aqalla in the accusative as the second object, with ana as an inserted separator.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «أقل» بالنصب على المفعول الثاني، وقوله أنا فاصلة ملغاة

rows.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: Isa b. Umar reads aqallu in the nominative, making ana the subject and aqallu its predicate; the vision here is inward.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى بن عمر: «أقل» بالرفع، على أن يكون أنا مبتدأ و «أقل» خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hope that God will give the believer something better may concern this world or the next; the afterlife reading is nobler and more conducive to good.
rows.anchor: وتمني ذلك في الآخرة أشرف مقطعا، وأذهب مع الخير والصلاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the hope concerns this life, it would sting the addressee more and hurt the believer himself more severely.
rows.anchor: وأن يكون ذلك يراد به الدنيا أذهب في نكاية المخاطب، وأشد إيلاما لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hisban is a punishment such as hail or a cold storm; the singular hasbana can denote missiles or volleys of projectiles.
rows.anchor: و «الحسبان» العذاب كالبرد والصر ونحوه، واحد الحسبان: حسبانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿid is the earth's surface; zalq is ground on which a foot cannot hold, stripped of growth and even the use of walking.
rows.anchor: و «الصعيد» وجه الأرض و «الزلق» الذي لا تثبت فيه قدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghawr is a verbal noun used adjectivally for water, whether singular or plural, and means water gone deep into the earth beyond reach.
rows.anchor: و «الغور» مصدر يوصف به الماء المفرد والمياه الكثيرة

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: The commentators cite variants with a damma on the ghayn and with a hamza; ghur, like Nuh, can describe singular or plural forms of either gender.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة «غورا» ، وقرأت فرقة «غورا» ، بضم الغين، وقرأت فرقة «غؤرا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line uses nuh as an adjective for horses, illustrating the form that can describe a group as well as an individual.
rows.anchor: تظل جيادها نوحا عليه ... مقلدة أعنتها صفونا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The calamity's encompassing the garden is a figure for the totality of its destruction and ruin.
rows.anchor: هذا خبر من الله عن إحاطة العذاب بحال هذا المثل به، وقد تقدم القول في الثمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning the palms means placing one palm against the back of the other, the gesture of regret; glossing it as clapping is inaccurate.
rows.anchor: يريد يضع بطن إحداهما على ظهر الأخرى، وذلك فعل المتلهف المتأسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trellises or roofs fell first, then the walls collapsed over them, leaving the garden hollow and ruined.
rows.anchor: يريد أن السقوف وقعت، وهي العروش، ثم تهدمت الحيطان عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators place the man's wish not to associate a partner with God in the afterlife; Ibn Atiyya allows that he said it in worldly repentance after the calamity as a warning to Quraysh and others.
rows.anchor: قال بعض المفسرين: هي حكاية عن قول الكافر هذه المقالة في الآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وعاصم وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers use the feminine verb for the group that could have helped him; Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Mujahid, and Ibn Waththab use masculine agreement by sense.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير ونافع وابن عامر وعاصم وأبو عمرو والحسن وأبو جعفر وشيبة: «ولم تكن» بالتاء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses the fiah, the group one relies on for aid, as one's clan.
rows.anchor: «الفئة» الجماعة التي يلجأ إلى نصرها، قال مجاهد هي العشيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly life in the parable means human life together with its blessings and comforts; the comparison says that it is like water.
rows.anchor: الحياة الدنيا يريد حياة الإنسان بما يتعلق بها من نعم وترفه، وقوله كماء يريد هي كماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vegetation mixed together because of the water; the bāʾ indicates cause, and aṣbaḥa means became rather than specifically morning.
rows.anchor: فاختلط به أي فاختلط النبات بعضه ببعض بسبب الماء، فالباء في به باء السبب

rows.speaker: الربيع بن ضبع
rows.claim: Rabīʿ b. Dabʿ's line shows aṣbaḥa used for a resulting state rather than a time of morning.
rows.anchor: أصبحت لا أحمل السلاح ولا ... أملك رأس البعير إن نفرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hasheem is brittle, fragmented dry vegetation; the word also underlies breaking up tharid, and tadhru means scatter.
rows.anchor: و «الهشيم» المتفتت من يابس العشب، ومنه قوله تعالى كهشيم المحتظر [القمر: 31]

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reads tadhrihi, meaning that the winds pull the vegetation up and cast it away; al-Hasan and others read wind in the singular.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس: «تذريه» ، والمعنى: تقلعه وترمي به

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh takes kāna as conveying that this was already the case before humans existed, something reason recognizes.
rows.anchor: هذا قول سيبويه، وهو معنى صحيح

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads kāna as reporting the state before created things existed: God's power already was.
rows.anchor: الحسن كان: إخبار عن الحال قبل إيجاد الموجودات، أي إن القدرة كانت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flourishing plant mirrors worldly beauty, power, and pride that fade, while a person's righteous work remains in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: فمن كان له عمل صالح، يبقى في الآخرة فهو الفائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling wealth and children adornment is qualified by the parable's belittling context: they adorn this devalued life and should not become one's chief desire.
rows.anchor: إنما المال والبنون زينة هذه الحياة المحقرة، فلا تتبعوها نفوسكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zina is a verbal noun predicated of concrete persons, so an omitted description must be supplied; the excerpt breaks off before giving it.
rows.anchor: وقوله زينة مصدر، وقد أخبر به عن أشخاص فإما أن يكون على تقدير محذوف، وتقديره:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment's fragment glosses a term as what is left by a flood, then shifts into the wording about presentation in rows.
rows.anchor: الترك، ومنه غدير الماء، وهو ما تركه السيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular ṣaffan stands for plural rows; sound reports describe all people gathered on one plain in rows and the people of Paradise as 120 ranks, 80 from this community.
rows.anchor: في الحديث الصحيح يجمع الله الأولين والآخرين في صعيد واحد صفوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address that the disbelievers have come as first created is a rebuke to those who denied resurrection; believers who accepted resurrection are not addressed this way.
rows.anchor: مقاولة للكفار المنكرين للبعث، ومضمنها التقريع والتوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording omits an understood clause such as it is said to the disbelievers among them, an ellipsis that improves concision.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام حذف ويقتضيه القول ويحسنه الإيجاز تقديره: يقال للكفرة منهم، ما خلقناكم أول مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's description of the resurrected as barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised explains the comparison with the first creation.
rows.anchor: يفسره قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إنكم تحشرون إلى الله حفاة عراة غرلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eyes here stand for insight: the intellect is veiled from remembrance and the law; inability to hear comes from turning away from and recoiling from the call to truth.
rows.anchor: أعينهم كناية عن البصائر، لأن عين الجارحة لا نسبة بينها وبين الذكر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read afahasiba with kasra on the sīn, meaning did they think; another reading with a still sīn and nominative bāʾ asks whether idols suffice as their goal.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس: «أفحسب الذين» بكسر السين بمعنى: أظنوا

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب والحسن وابن يعمر ومجاهد
rows.claim: These readers use the alternative afahasbu, meaning are the idols their sufficient end or goal; Ibn Masud's codex supports the majority reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي بن أبي طالب والحسن وابن يعمر ومجاهد وابن كثير بخلاف عنه: «أفحسب» بسكون السين

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: The servants worshipped besides God include angels, Ezra, and Jesus; the disbelievers include some Arabs, Jews, and Christians, who will gain no benefit from them.
rows.anchor: يريد كل من عبد من دون الله كالملائكة وعزير وعيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿtadna means prepared; nuzul can be a lodging place or food offered to a guest, perhaps ironically making Hell their provision.
rows.anchor: وأعتدنا معناه: يسرنا، و «النزل» موضع النزول، و «النزل» أيضا ما يقدم للضيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about the greatest losers is a taunting rebuke addressed to the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: ثم قال تعالى: هل ننبئكم بالأخسرين أعمالا الآية المعنى: قل لهؤلاء الكفرة على جهة التوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who say God has taken a child include Arab polytheists calling angels His daughters, Christians, and everyone who makes this kind of claim.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قالوا للكفار من العرب في قولهم للملائكة بنات الله وللنصارى ولكل من كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idd means a terrible, difficult, and outrageous matter; the address to them is understood as say this to them.
rows.anchor: و «الإد» الأمر الشنيع الصعب وهي الدواهي والشنع العظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says that when this claim was first made, trees groaned or split, Hell blazed, and the angels became angry.
rows.anchor: ويروى عن النبي عليه السلام أن هذه المقالة أول ما قيلت في العالم شاك الشجر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read iddan with kasra on the hamza; Abu Abd al-Rahman reads it with fatḥa, and the forms idd, add, and ādd are related.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور، «إدا» بكسر الهمزة، وقرأ أبو عبد الرحمن «أدا» بفتح الهمزة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads takādu with feminine tāʾ and yatfattaṛna with the intensified verb; other readers vary between this and yanfaṭirna.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير هنا وفي حم عسق «تكاد» بالتاء «يتفطرن» بياء وتاء وفتح الطاء

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says takādu can mean intends, as in akādu ukhfiha; Ibn Atiyya finds the poetic proof insufficient and calls the analysis unstable.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحسن الأخفش «تكاد» بمعنى تريد، وكذلك قوله تعالى أكاد أخفيها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority treat the near rupture of heaven, earth, and mountains as a metaphor for the enormity of the claim, following a familiar Arab rhetorical pattern.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور: إنما هي استعارة لشنعة الأمر أي هذا حقه لو فهمت الجمادات قدره

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarir's line about city walls and mountains bowing at news of al-Zubayr illustrates this metaphorical expression.
rows.anchor: لما أتى خبر الزبير تواضعت ... سور المدينة والجبال الخشع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning means that God similarly punishes those who exceed bounds and disbelieve.
rows.anchor: وكما وصفنا من أليم الأفعال نجزي المسرفين المتعدين الكفار بالله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the constricted life is in this world or the barzakh, the verse adds an afterlife threat; if it is already in the afterlife, it reiterates that its punishment surpasses imaginable worldly pain.
rows.anchor: إن كانت معيشة الضنك في الدنيا أو البرزخ فجاء هذا وعيدا في الآخرة بعد وعيد

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: For the reading yahdi, one group makes kam the subject, but Basran grammarians reject this because kam must begin the clause; Ibn Masud's man ahlakna reading supports the analysis.
rows.anchor: واختلفت هذه الفرقة في الفاعل فقال بعضها الفاعل كم وهذا قول كوفي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj makes God the subject: God has shown them the signs and lessons, with the verb attributed to Him.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم الفاعل الله عز وجل، والمعنى أفلم يهد لهم ما جعل الله لهم من الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other grammarians supply an implicit subject such as guidance, the affair, reflection, or consideration; a nun reading fits the interpretation with God as subject.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم الفاعل مقدر الهدى أو الأمرع أو النظر أو الاعتبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nations are Ad, Thamud, and other peoples whose ruined settlements Quraysh passed on journeys toward Syria.
rows.anchor: فإنما أراد عادا أو ثمود أو الطوائف التي كانت قريش تجوز على بلادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuha is the plural of nuhya, the faculty that restrains a person from shameful action.
rows.anchor: والنهى جمع نهية وهو ما ينهى الإنسان عن فعل القبيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prior divine word delayed the binding punishment to an appointed term; the possible term is resurrection, each person's death, or Badr, with corresponding afterlife, grave, or military punishment.
rows.anchor: واختلف الناس في الأجل فيحتمل أن يريد يوم القيامة والعذاب المتوعد به على هذا هو عذاب جهنم

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group identifies the binding punishment with Badr, citing a report in Sahih al-Bukhari; Ibn Atiyya says this reading is especially eloquent as a sign of the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح البخاري، أن يوم بدر وهو اللزام وهو البطشة الكبرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to endure their accusations that he is a sorcerer, soothsayer, or liar, since their destruction is coming.
rows.anchor: ثم أمره تعالى بالصبر على أقوالهم إنه ساحر وإنه كاهن وإنه كذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most interpreters identify the times as five prayers: dawn before sunrise, afternoon before sunset, Isha in the night, and Maghrib and Dhuhr at the day's edges.
rows.anchor: الخمس قبل طلوع الشمس صلاة الصبح وقبل غروبها صلاة العصر ومن آناء الليل

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group assigns Maghrib and Isha to the night and Dhuhr alone to the day's edges.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة آناء الليل المغرب والعشاء، وأطراف النهار الظهر وحدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording may instead refer to saying subhan Allah wa bihamdihi after dawn until the two rakas of duha and before sunset; a prophetic report promises forgiveness for seventy glorifications before sunset.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل اللفظ أن يراد قول سبحان الله وبحمده من بعد صلاة الصبح إلى ركعتي الضحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural edges can reflect dual phrasing like your hearts, the generic recurrence of a day, or the two halves of daylight divided at noon; Ibn Furak notes the last analysis.
rows.anchor: وسمى الطرفين أطرافا على أحد وجهين إما على نحو فقد صغت قلوبكما

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: The poetic line uses ana for an hour of the night, supporting the explanation of anāʾ as times.
rows.anchor: والآناء جمع أنى وهي الساعة من الليل ومنه قول الهذلي

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the verse as referring to voluntary prayers, including night prayers, the two pre-dawn rakas, and Maghrib.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة في الآية إشارة إلى نوافل، فمنها آناء الليل ومنها قبل طلوع الشمس

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read tarḍa with fatḥa, so that the Prophet may be rewarded with what satisfies him.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «لعلك ترضى» بفتح التاء أي لعلك تثاب على هذه الأعمال بما ترضى به

rows.speaker: الكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: These readers use ḍamma on the tāʾ, meaning that the Prophet will be given what pleases him.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم «لعلك ترضى» أي لعلك تعطى ما يرضيك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: The verse concerns wavering Bedouins who stayed Muslim when wealth or a son came, but took hardship as an omen and apostatized, as the ʿUrayniyyun did.
rows.anchor: قال هذا المعنى ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worshipping on an edge means leaning away from the clear faith or standing on its brink, about to fall away.
rows.anchor: على حرف معناه على انحراف منه عن العقيدة البيضاء أو على شفى منها معدى للزهوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fitna here means a test; turning back on one's face means loss in worldly circumstances and, through apostasy and bad belief, in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: الاختبار، وقوله تعالى: انقلب على وجهه عبارة للمولي عن الأمور وخسارته الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وحميد والأعرج
rows.claim: These readers use the accusative khāsiran as a circumstantial expression for losing both this world and the next.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وحميد والأعرج «خاسرا الدنيا والآخرة» نصبا على الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objects called upon are idols; yadʿu can mean worshipping them or invoking them in distress.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: ما لا يضره يريد الأوثان، ومعنى يدعوا يعبد، ويدعو أيضا في ملماته

rows.speaker: فرقة من الكوفيين
rows.claim: A Kufan group says the lām is displaced and the intended wording is yadʿu man la-ḍaruhu; Ibn Masud's reading supports it.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة من الكوفيين اللام مقدمة على موضعها وإنما التقدير «يدعو من لضره»

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash takes yadʿu to mean says and parses a clause about one whose harm is nearer than benefit; Ibn Atiyya rejects it because an idolater would not believe this.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش يدعوا يمعنى يقول، و «من» مبتدأ وضره مبتدأ، وأقرب خبره

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj permits yadʿu as a circumstantial clause with an omitted pronoun, while Abu Ali proposes a relative reading of dhalika that Ibn Atiyya finds difficult.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج يجوز أن يكون يدعوا في موضع الحال وفيه هاء محذوفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yadʿu may continue the preceding rebuke, then restart with liman ḍarruhu; the lām signals an oath and the second lām is also oath-marking.
rows.anchor: وقد يظهر في الآية أن يكون قوله يدعوا متصلا بما قبله، ويكون فيه معنى التوبيخ

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali also considers attaching the verb to the lām through a verb that licenses a complement; Ibn Atiyya notes that the analysis is disputed.
rows.anchor: ويظهر أيضا في الآية أن يكون المراد يدعو من ضره ثم علق الفعل باللام

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari identifies the patron and intimate companion as the conditional worshipper himself; Ibn Atiyya prefers the idol as the referent because its harm exceeds its benefit.
rows.anchor: وذهب الطبري إلى أن المراد بالمولى والعشير هو الإنسان الذي يعبد الله على حرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hatta introduces the passage, though it might mark an endpoint with omitted material; the direct introductory reading better fits what is meant to be discussed.
rows.anchor: حتى في هذا الموضع حرف ابتداء ويحتمل أن تكون غاية مجردة بتقدير كلام محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dead person is a disbeliever; irjiʿuni asks to return to worldly life, and the plural may magnify God's address or shift from calling God to addressing the punishing angels.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله أحدهم للكفار، وقوله ارجعون معناه إلى الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the dead person in this verse is a polytheist.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك هي في المشرك

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report to Aisha says the believer, when seeing death, chooses to go forward to God rather than return to the house of grief, while the unbeliever asks to return and do good.
rows.anchor: وقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، لعائشة

rows.speaker: الحسن والجمهور
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and the majority use a still yā in laʿalli; Talha b. Musarrif opens it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والجمهور «لعلي» بسكون الياء، وقرأ طلحة بن مصرف «لعلي» بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla is a divine rejection and rebuke; the phrase that follows has three possible senses: a prediction, an empty utterance, or proof that a returned person would relapse.
rows.anchor: وكلا رد وزجر وهي من كلام الله تعالى، وقوله إنها كلمة هو قائلها يحتمل ثلاثة معان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh literally means a barrier between two distances and here denotes the period between death and resurrection, as the exegetes agree.
rows.anchor: و «البرزخ» ، في كلام العرب الحاجز بين المسافتين، ثم يستعار لما عدا ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The majority read al-sur as the trumpet; Ibn Abbas reads al-suwar with a fatḥa on the wāw, meaning images or forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «في الصور» وهو القرن، وقرأ ابن عباس «الصور» بفتح الواو جمع صورة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others place the loss of kinship at the first trumpet, when everyone dies; Ibn Atiyya objects that this removes the verse's reference to the terror of gathering.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس وغيره: هذا في النفخة الأولى وذلك أن الناس بأجمعهم يموتون

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud and others say kinship no longer helps after the second trumpet because people are overwhelmed and each is occupied with himself; Ibn Atiyya calls this interpretation good.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود وغيره: إنما المعنى أنه عند النفخة الثانية وقيام الناس من القبور

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says a person will fear anyone he recognizes because of a possible unpaid grievance; people flee relatives, and everyone is glad to have a claim against family.
rows.anchor: وروي عن قتادة أنه قال: ليس أحد أبغض إلى الإنسان في ذلك اليوم ممن يعرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Questioning and recognition are also absent during this overwhelming stage, although later scenes of resurrection include questions and recognition.
rows.anchor: وكذلك ارتفاع التساؤل والتعارف لهذه الوجوه التي ذكرناها ثم تأتي في القيامة مواطن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heavy scales mean good deeds outweighing; weight and lightness apply to forms God creates to embody deeds, according to reports.
rows.anchor: و «ثقل الموازين» هو الحسنات، والثقل والخفة إنما يتعلق بأجرام يخترع الله فيها ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawazin is plural because the weighed things, the deeds, are plural; weighing makes the proof tangible in familiar human terms.
rows.anchor: جمع «الموازين» من حيث الموزون جمع وهي الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A disbeliever's unbelief may be placed against an empty pan, or against good deeds such as charity to kin, which it outweighs.
rows.anchor: إما أن يوضع كفره في كفة فلا يجد شيئا يعادله في الكفة الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lafh means the fire's scorching heat; Abu Haywa's kalihun without alif describes lips drawn back to expose teeth, like singed rams' heads.
rows.anchor: و «لفح النار» إصابتها بالوهج والإحراق، وقرأ أبو حيوة «كلحون» بغير ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about God's signs has an omitted introduction, namely that it is said to them; the signs here are the Quran.
rows.anchor: وقوله ألم تكن آياتي قبله محذوف تقديره يقال لهم، و «الآيات» هنا القرآن

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read shaqwatuna with kasra and no extra alif; Hamza and al-Kisaʾi read shaqawatuna with fatḥa and an alif, while Asim permits both.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «شقوتنا» بكسر الشين دون ألف بعد القاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After admitting guilt, they move to pleading; confession is an apology and disavowal, but God's decreed reply is to drive them away and silence them.
rows.anchor: ثم تدرجوا من الإقرار إلى الرغبة والتضرع وذلك أنهم ذلوا لأن الإقرار بالذنب اعتذار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya abbreviates al-Tabari's long dialogue between the disbelievers, Hell's keeper, and God because he considers its report unsound, though its meaning is sound.
rows.anchor: واختصرت هذا الحديث لعدم صحته لكن معناه صحيح عافانا الله من ناره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhsau is a rebuke used to drive away dogs; the Prophet used it to Ibn Sayyad, telling him he would not exceed his station.
rows.anchor: وقوله اخسؤا زجر يستعمل في زجر الكلاب، ومنه قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لابن صياد اخسأ فلن تعدو قدرك

rows.speaker: نافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers have qala kam labithtum and qul in labithtum; other readers vary between a command or report for the first verb.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر «قال كم لبثتم» و «قل إن لبثتم»

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi use qul for both questions and statements, while al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir has a command for the question and a report for the answer.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي فيهما «قل لكم لبثتم» و «قل إن لبثتم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings mean either God asks and then tells them the stay was brief, an individual is ordered to answer and corrected, or they are questioned before being told the answer.
rows.anchor: فمعنى الأول إخبار عن الله بوقفهم بالسؤال عن المدة ثم يعلمهم آخرا بلبثهم قليلا

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari understands their stay in the earth as their living time in this world; they have forgotten through torment and estimate only a day or part of one.
rows.anchor: وقوله في الأرض قال الطبري معناه في الدنيا أحياء وعن هذا وقع السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya prefers the time they lay dead in the earth, since they denied resurrection and are now asked after rising from the soil.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الأصوب من حيث أنكروا البعث، وكان قوله إنهم لا يقومون من التراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The point is that their lives were brief but disbelief led them to long punishment; ʿadad is a specification after kam, and al-Aʿmash reads it with tanwin.
rows.anchor: والغرض من هذا توقيفهم على أن أعمارهم قصيرة أداهم الكفر فيها إلى عذاب طويل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the counters they tell to ask are the angels; Qatada says they mean people who calculate.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد أرادوا ب العادين الملائكة، وقال قتادة أرادوا أهل الحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording does not specify angels or anyone else; it asks generally for whoever can count, since a sleeping or dead person does not measure time's passing.
rows.anchor: وظاهر اللفظ أنهم أرادوا سل من يتصف بهذه الصفة، ولم يعينوا ملائكة ولا غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their stay is brief relative to torment if it was worldly life, or brief because what is coming is near if it was the grave; ʿabathan means purposelessly, and the two readings of tarjiʿun have the same sense.
rows.anchor: وقوله إن لبثتم إلا قليلا مقصده على القول بأن اللبث في الدنيا، أي قليل القدر في جنب ما تعذبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vision is sight by the eye; the implied focus is God's command and power.
rows.anchor: الرؤية في هذه الآية رؤية عين والتقدير أن أمر الله وقدرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yuzji means to drive slowly, used for moving heavy or sluggish things such as clouds and camels.
rows.anchor: ويزجي معناه يسوق، والإزجاء إنما يستعمل في سوق كل ثقيل ومدافعته كالسحاب والإبل المزاحف

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line about slow camels that yuzji-hā illustrates the verb's sense of driving them along.
rows.anchor: على مزاحيف تزجيها مخارير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about merchandise of little value refers to goods requiring intercession and promotion to get them moving, like a heavy load.
rows.anchor: والبضاعة المزجاة التي تحتاج من الشفاعة والتحسين إلى ما هو كسوق الثقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yuliffu combines dispersed clouds; the construction between them reflects the gaps inherent in clouds, and between cannot normally take a singular without another item understood.
rows.anchor: وقوله يؤلف بينه أي بين مفترق السحاب نفسه لأن مفهوم السحاب يقتضي أن بينه فروجا

rows.speaker: ورش
rows.claim: Warsh from Nafi does not use hamza in yūlif; Qalun and the other readers pronounce the hamza, which is the basic form.
rows.anchor: وورش عن نافع لا يهمز «يولف» وقالون عن نافع والباقون يهمزون «يؤلف»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rukam is piled and compacted cloud; wind compresses it so rain comes out, as in the verse about water pouring from the clouds.
rows.anchor: و «الركام» الذي يركب بعضه بعضا ويتكاثف

rows.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
rows.claim: Hassan's poem about pressed juice compares wine to water pressed from clouds; the Basran judge used it to explain the verse to a litigant.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قول حسان بن ثابت: [الكامل] كلتاهما حلب العصير ... فعاطني بزجاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wadq means rain, as in a poet's description of a cloud releasing its rain and the earth sprouting.
rows.anchor: والودق المطر ومنه قول الشاعر: [المتقارب] فلا مزنة ودقت ودقها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read min khilalihi, the plural of khalal; Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak read min khallihi, while Asim and al-Aʿraj intensify yunazzilu.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس «من خلاله» وهو جمع خلل كجبل وجبال

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Some take the mountains of hail literally, while others use mountains as a metaphor for abundant hail; al-Akhfash's claim that min before barad is extra is weak.
rows.anchor: وقوله من جبال فيها من برد قيل تلك حقيقة وقد جعل الله تعالى في السماء جبالا من برد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositions distinguish source from heaven, partitive selection from the mountains, and the kind or substance of the hail.
rows.anchor: ومن في قوله من السماء هي لابتداء الغاية، وفي قوله «من الجبال» هي للتبعيض

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Sana without hamza means light, while sanaʾ with a long vowel means glory or elevation; most read the short form and Talha the long one.
rows.anchor: و «السنا» ، مقصور، الضوء والسناء، ممدود، المجد والارتفاع في المنزلة

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Talha reads barqihi as baruqihi, a collective for flashes of lightning, and reads the word with a long hamza as well.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة أيضا «برقة» بضم الباء وفتح الراء وهي جمع «برقة» بضم الباء وسكون الراء

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reads yudhhibu with ḍamma, from adh haba; the bāʾ may indicate an appropriate action or resemble a construction with an extra bāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر «يذهب» بضمها من أذهب كأن التقدير يذهب النفوس بالأبصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unprepared transition to God's rotation of night and day is itself beyond eloquent speakers, who need verbal arrangement and introduction.
rows.anchor: والإتيان بهذا بعد هذا دون توطئة هو الذي تعجز عنه الفصحاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccans asked about the name al-Rahman as though it were unknown, so the passage states recognizable divine attributes that require acknowledgment of lordship.
rows.anchor: لما جعلت قريش سؤالها عن الله تعالى وعن اسمه الذي هو الرحمن سؤالا عن مجهول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The constellations are familiar celestial stations used in reckoning time; each is two and one-third lunar mansions, linked to the moon's stations.
rows.anchor: وكل برج منها على منزلتين وثلث من منازل القمر التي ذكرها الله تعالى في قوله والقمر قدرناه منازل

rows.speaker: الأخطل
rows.claim: Al-Akhtal's line compares a structure to a Roman tower built of lime, brick, and stone, showing the earthly sense of burj.
rows.anchor: كأنها برج رومي يشيده ... لز بجص وآجور وأحجار

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Some say the constellations are palaces in Paradise; Ibn Masud's companions read palaces in heaven, and al-Aʿmash transmits another view that they are great stars.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعمش: كان أصحاب عبد الله يقرؤونها «في السماء قصورا»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Paradise-palace interpretation weakens the verse's purpose, which is to point to observable signs that establish proof for deniers and the ignorant.
rows.anchor: وأما القول بأنها قصور في الجنة فقول يحط غرض الآية في التنبيه على أشياء مدركات

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read sirajan as the sun; Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Ibn Masud, Alqama, and al-Aʿmash read surujan for all lights, then the moon is named specially.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «سراجا» وهي الشمس، وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وعبد الله بن مسعود وعلقمة والأعمش «سرجا»

rows.speaker: النخعي وابن وثاب والأعمش
rows.claim: These readers have a form with a still rāʾ; Abu Hatim and Abu Amr report a variant reading of the moon term as a plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ النخعي وابن وثاب والأعمش «سرجا» بسكون الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khilfa means that night and day succeed one another, each replacing the other.
rows.anchor: وقوله خلفة أي هذا يخلف هذا، وهذا يخلف هذا

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr's cited line illustrates the changing night and day by depicting every creature moving slowly and seeking its prey.
rows.anchor: كلهم يمشي رويدا ... كلهم يطلب صيدا

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri says swift walking takes away the face's beauty; Ibn Atiyya specifies that he means hurried haste, since moderation preserves dignity.
rows.anchor: وقال الزهري سرعة المشي تذهب ببهاء الوجه

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd b. Aslam recounts a dream in which he was told that those who walk gently are people who do not seek to corrupt the earth.
rows.anchor: فرأيت في النوم من جاءني فقال هم الذين لا يريدون أن يفسدوا في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hunan means gently and moderately; the Prophet's saying to love someone moderately supports this sense.
rows.anchor: وهونا معناه رفقا وقصدا، ومنه قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم «أجب حبيبك هونا ما» الحديث

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group takes salaman as the literal word peace or farewell, with a verb understood from the same root.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة ينبغي للمخاطب أن يقول للجاهل سلاما بهذا اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says qalu itself governs salaman: the sense is that they utter this phrase.
rows.anchor: والذي أقول إن قالوا هو العامل في سلاما لأن المعنى قالوا هذا اللفظ

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets salaman as a sound, straight statement used to repel the ignorant with gentleness and soft words.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد معنى سلاما قولا سديدا، أي يقول للجاهل كلاما يدفعه به برفق ولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse predates the sword verse: what addresses unbelievers was abrogated, while its etiquette among Muslims remains; Ibn Atiyya follows Sibawayh in taking it as peace or safety rather than a greeting to unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية كانت قبل آية السيف فنسخ منها ما يختص الكفرة وبقي أدبها في المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A historical anecdote says Ibrahim b. al-Mahdi dreamed that Ali answered his complaint with salaman; al-Maʾmun identified the Quranic response and Ibrahim was embarrassed.
rows.anchor: فقال المأمون وبماذا جاوبك قال: فكان يقول لي سلاما سلاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya concludes that Ibrahim's vision was undoubtedly true and Ali's answer was the most eloquent response.
rows.anchor: فحزن إبراهيم واستحيا وكانت رؤياه لا محالة صحيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind's stirring is moving clouds from rest and driving them onward; spreading them in the sky means dispersing them, and kisaf means pieces.
rows.anchor: «الإثارة» تحريكها من سكونها وتسييرها، وبسطه في السماء هو نشره في الآفاق

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read kisafan with fatḥa on the sīn; Ibn Abbas and others use the still-sīn form, both collective plurals.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور القراء «كسفا» بفتح السين

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki says the still-sīn reading means that God makes the cloud a single piece.
rows.anchor: وقال مكي: من أسكن السين فمعناه يجعل السحاب قطعة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wadq means rain, and khilal means the spaces between the cloud's loosely joined parts; poetry illustrates wadq.
rows.anchor: والودق الماء يمطر ومنه قول الشاعر: [المتقارب] فلا مزنة ودقت ودقها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read min khilalihi as a plural of khalal; Ali, Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Hasan also read the collective noun min khallihi.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «من خلاله» بكسر الخاء وألف بعد اللام جمع خلل كجبل وجبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in khilalihi can refer to the cloud or, with the still-sīn reading, to its pieces; with fatḥa on sīn it refers only to the cloud.
rows.anchor: والضمير في خلاله يحتمل أن يعود على السحاب ويحتمل أن يعود على الكسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated min qablihi emphasizes how quickly people's hearts move from despair to joy when rain arrives.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: من قبله تأكيد أفاد سرعة تقلب قلوب البشر من الإبلاس إلى الاستبشار

rows.speaker: يعقوب وعيسى وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers lighten the zāy in yunzilu; Ibn Masud omits min qablihi, and iblas means misery with no hope of relief.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يعقوب وعيسى وأبو عمرو بخلاف عنه «ينزل» مخففة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers use the singular athar; Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi use the plural athār, while other variants are also reported.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو «أثر» بالإفراد

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: In one reading, how the earth is revived may have earth as its subject or be a circumstantial phrase meaning reviving it; drought and greening are figurative death and life.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الفتح: قوله «كيف تحيى» جملة منصوبة الموضع على الحال حملا على المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revived land is an analogy and reminder of resurrection, and God's power over everything is universal.
rows.anchor: ثم أخبر تعالى على جهة القياس والتنبيه عليه بالبعث والنشور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human life cycle is another sign showing that idols have no part in these transformations.
rows.anchor: وهذه أيضا عبر بين فيها أن الأوثان لا مدخل لها فيها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce weakness with ḍamma; Asim and Hamza read it with fatḥa, but Ibn Atiyya prefers the ḍamma form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور القراء والناس بضم الضاد في «ضعف» ، وقرأ عاصم وحمزة بفتحها

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports that the Prophet corrected his recitation with fatḥa to the ḍamma reading; grammarians also distinguish bodily weakness by ḍamma from mental weakness by fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عمر أنه قرأ على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالفتح فردها عليه بالضم

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن والجحدري والضحاك
rows.claim: These readers use ḍamma on the first two occurrences and fatḥa on the final one; Isa b. Umar uses two dammas.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي عبد الرحمن والجحدري والضحاك أنهم ضموا الضاد في الأول والثاني وفتحو «ضعفا»

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The first weakness is the human origin from impure fluid, strength is youth and robust vigor, and the second weakness is old age.
rows.anchor: و «الضعف» الأول هو كون الإنسان من ماء مهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The criminals swear stubbornly and without knowledge that they stayed under the earth less than an hour, continuing their worldly habit of false reasoning; yufakun means turned from truth.
rows.anchor: أن المجرمين يقسمون لجاجا منهم وتسورا على ما لا علم لهم به أنهم ما لبثوا تحت التراب

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Some say they mean their worldly life seemed brief after they saw the afterlife; Ibn Atiyya rejects this because the verse says they were habitually turned away from truth.
rows.anchor: وقيل المعنى ما لبثوا في الدنيا كأنهم استقلوها لما عاينوا من أمر الآخرة

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some interpreters take the wording as fronting faith and postponing knowledge.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المفسرين: إنما أراد أوتوا الإيمان والعلم ففي الكلام تقديم وتأخير
